questions.question_text:
The table below shows corresponding values of x and y for y = sqrt(x/(1+x)). The values of y are given to 4 significant figures.
x: 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5
y: 0.5774, 0.7071, 0.7746, 0.8165, 0.8452

(a) Use the trapezium rule, with all the values of y in the table, to find an estimate for ∫[0.5 to 2.5] sqrt(x/(1+x)) dx, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. (3)

(b) Using your answer to part (a), deduce an estimate for ∫[0.5 to 2.5] sqrt(9x/(1+x)) dx. (1)

Given that ∫[0.5 to 2.5] sqrt(9x/(1+x)) dx = 4.535 to 4 significant figures,
(c) comment on the accuracy of your answer to part (b). (1)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: States or uses h = 0.5 (may be implied within the trapezium rule calculation). M1: Correct attempt at the trapezium rule: (1/2)h*{first y + last y + 2*(sum of the middle y values)} = (0.5/2){0.5774 + 0.8452 + 2(0.7071 + 0.7746 + 0.8165)}, condoning slips on the terms but must use all y values with no repeats and a clear attempt at the (1/2)h(first+last+2*rest) structure. A1: awrt 1.50 (apply isw if necessary). (3 marks)
(b) B1ft: 3 × their (a). If (a) is correct, allow awrt 4.50 or awrt 4.51 even with no working; only allow 4.5 if (a) is correct and working is shown e.g. 3×1.5. If (a) is incorrect allow 3×their(a) given to at least 3sf. (1 mark)
(c) B1: This mark depends on the B1 having been awarded in part (b) with awrt 4.5. Look for a sensible comment about accuracy, e.g. 'accurate to 2sf/1dp', 'underestimate but close', or a correctly calculated percentage error using awrt 4.50 or 4.51 (e.g. (4.535-4.50)/4.535×100 = 0.77%). Mark withheld if there are contradictory statements. (1 mark)
questions.notes: The formula for y was rendered in the PDF text without the square-root sign. Reconstructed as y = sqrt(x/(1+x)) because this exactly reproduces every tabulated y value (e.g. sqrt(0.5/1.5)=0.5774, sqrt(2.5/3.5)=0.8452), and part (b)'s integrand sqrt(9x/(1+x)) = 3*sqrt(x/(1+x)) explains why the mark scheme uses '3 × their (a)'.

questions.question_text: Relative to a fixed origin, points P, Q and R have position vectors p, q and r respectively. Given that P, Q and R lie on a straight line, and Q lies one third of the way from P to R, show that q = (1/3)(r + 2p). (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text: M1: Attempts any of the relevant vectors by subtracting either way around, e.g. ±PQ = ±(q-p), ±PR = ±(r-p), ±QR = ±(r-q) (may be implied by sight of any one of these, ignoring how they are labelled). dM1: Uses the given information and writes it correctly in vector form that if rearranged would give the printed answer, e.g. r - q = 2(q - p), or r - p = 3(q - p), or (2/3)(q-p) = (1/3)(r-q). A1*: Fully correct work leading to the given answer, e.g. r - q = 2q - 2p => 2p + r = 3q => q = (1/3)(r + 2p). Allow OQ = ... as long as OQ has been defined as q earlier; allow use of P instead of p and Q instead of q as long as the intention is clear. (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
(a) Given that 2 log(4 - x) = log(x + 8), show that x^2 - 9x + 8 = 0. (3)
(b) (i) Write down the roots of the equation x^2 - 9x + 8 = 0.
(ii) State which of the roots in (b)(i) is not a solution of 2 log(4 - x) = log(x + 8), giving a reason for your answer. (2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: States or uses 2 log(4-x) = log((4-x)^2). M1: Correct attempt at eliminating the logs to form a quadratic equation in x, e.g. (4-x)^2 = x + 8. A1*: Proceeds to the given answer x^2 - 9x + 8 = 0 with at least one line where (4-x)^2 has been multiplied out; there must be no errors or omissions (condone invisible brackets around the arguments of the logs). (3 marks)
(b)(i) B1: (x =) 1, 8. (ii) B1: 8 is not a solution as log(4 - 8) cannot be found — must refer to the 8 as the value being rejected and give a reason referring to log(4-x)/log of the lhs being undefined for a negative argument (e.g. 'log(-4) can't be worked out/is undefined/gives a math error'); no contradictory statements allowed. (2 marks)

questions.question_text: In the binomial expansion of (a + 2x)^7, where a is a constant, the coefficient of x^4 is 15120. Find the value of a. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text: M1: Attempt at the correct coefficient of x^4: this must have the correct binomial coefficient (7C4), the correct power of a (a^3), and 2^4 or 24 (may be implied), e.g. (7C4) a^3 (2x)^4, 35a^3(2x)^4, 560a^3x^4. dM1: For '560'a^3 = 15120 => a = ... (condone slips on copying the 15120, but their '560' must be an attempt at 7C4 × 2^4, and they must attempt the cube root of 15120/'560'; depends on the first mark). A1: a = 3, and no other values (i.e. a = ±3 scores A0). (3 marks)

questions.question_text: The curve with equation y = 3 × 2^x meets the curve with equation y = 15 - 2^(x+1) at the point P. Find, using algebra, the exact x coordinate of P. (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text: B1: Combines the equations to reach 15 - 2^(x+1) = 3 × 2^x, or equivalent. M1: Uses 2^(x+1) = 2 × 2^x to obtain an equation in 2^x and attempts to make 2^x the subject, reaching 2^x = 3. dM1: Uses logs correctly and proceeds to a value for x from an equation of the form 2^x = k (k > 1), e.g. 2^x = k => x = log_2(k) (depends on the first method mark; may be implied if they go straight to decimals e.g. 2^x = 3 so x = 1.584...). A1cso: x = log_2(3), or log3/log2, or ln3/ln2 (ignore any attempts to find the y-coordinate). (4 marks)
questions.notes: The exponents 'x' and 'x+1' were extracted onto separate lines above the question text by the PDF converter; reconstructed as y=3×2^x and y=15-2^(x+1) since this exactly matches the mark scheme's working (15-2^(x+1)=3×2^x, then 2^(x+1)=2×2^x).

questions.question_text:
(a) Given that (x^2 + 8x - 3)/(x + 2) ≡ Ax + B + C/(x + 2), x ∈ R, x ≠ -2, find the values of the constants A, B and C. (3)
(b) Hence, using algebraic integration, find the exact value of ∫[0 to 6] (x^2 + 8x - 3)/(x + 2) dx, giving your answer in the form a + b ln 2 where a and b are integers to be found. (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Multiplies by (x+2) and attempts to find values for A, B and C, e.g. by comparing coefficients or substituting values for x (or attempts to divide x^2+8x-3 by x+2 to obtain a linear quotient and constant remainder); may be implied by 2 correct values for A, B or C. A1: Two of A = 1, B = 6, C = -15 (just performing the division correctly is insufficient — A, B, C must be clearly identified). A1: All three of A = 1, B = 6, C = -15 (may be implied by stating (x^2+8x-3)/(x+2) = x + 6 - 15/(x+2), or within the integral in (b)). (3 marks)
(b) M1: Integrates an expression of the form C/(x+2) to obtain k ln(x+2) (condone the omission of brackets around 'x+2'). A1ft: Correct integration, follow through on their Ax + B + C/(x+2) (A,B,C ≠ 0): (1/2)x^2 + 6x - 15 ln(x+2) (+c) (brackets should be present around 'x+2' unless implied by subsequent work). M1: Substitutes both limits 0 and 6 into an expression containing an x or x^2 term (or both) and a ln term, and subtracts either way round, WITH fully correct log work to combine the two log terms (allowing sign errors when removing brackets), leading to an answer of the form a + b ln c (a, b, c not necessarily integers). A1: 54 - 30 ln 2 (apply isw once a correct answer is seen). (4 marks)

questions.question_text:
Figure 1 shows a sketch of the curve C with equation y = (4x^2 + x)/(2 sqrt(x)) - 4 ln x, x > 0.
(a) Show that dy/dx = (12x^2 + x - 16 sqrt(x))/(4x sqrt(x)). (4)
The point P, shown in Figure 1, is the minimum turning point on C.
(b) Show that the x coordinate of P is a solution of x = (4/3 - sqrt(x)/12)^(2/3). (3)
(c) Use the iteration formula x_(n+1) = (4/3 - sqrt(x_n)/12)^(2/3), with x_1 = 2, to find (i) the value of x_2 to 5 decimal places, (ii) the x coordinate of P to 5 decimal places. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: Differentiates ln x -> 1/x (seen or implied). M1: Correct method to differentiate (4x^2+x)/(2 sqrt(x)): look for (4x^2+x)/(2 sqrt(x)) -> ...x^(3/2) + ...x^(1/2) being then differentiated to Px^(1/2) + ...x^(-1/2), or a correct application of the quotient rule on (4x^2+x) and 2 sqrt(x), or the product rule on (4x^2+x)(2 sqrt(x))^(-1); condone slips but a correct rule may be implied by their u, v, u', v' followed by applying (vu'-uv')/v^2. A1: Correct differentiation of (4x^2+x)/(2 sqrt(x)) (may not be simplified). A1*: Obtains dy/dx = (12x^2+x-16sqrt(x))/(4x sqrt(x)) via 3sqrt(x) + 1/(2sqrt(x)) - 4/x, or a correct application of the quotient/product rule, with sufficient working shown and no errors (e.g. missing brackets) to reach the printed answer. (4 marks)
(b) M1: Sets 12x^2 + x - 16 sqrt(x) = 0 and divides by sqrt(x) (or equivalent, e.g. divides by x and multiplies by sqrt(x)). dM1: Makes the term in x^(3/2) the subject of the formula. A1*: A correct and rigorous argument leading to the given solution x = (4/3 - sqrt(x)/12)^(2/3). (3 marks)
(c) M1: Attempts to use the iterative formula with x_1 = 2 (implied by sight of x_2 = (4/3 - sqrt(2)/12)^(2/3), or awrt 1.14). A1: x_2 = awrt 1.13894. A1: Deduces that x = 1.15650 (the x coordinate of P). (3 marks)
questions.notes: The iteration formula in parts (b) and (c) was heavily garbled by the PDF extraction (exponents/fraction layout scattered across lines). Reconstructed as x = (4/3 - sqrt(x)/12)^(2/3) [and the analogous iteration x_(n+1) = (4/3 - sqrt(x_n)/12)^(2/3)] by working forward algebraically from the part (a) derivative set to zero and cross-checking against the mark scheme notes ('divides by sqrt(x)', 'makes the term in x^(3/2) the subject', and the numeric check x_2 = awrt 1.13894 matching (4/3-sqrt(2)/12)^(2/3)).

questions.question_text: A curve C has equation y = f(x). Given that f'(x) = 6x^2 + ax - 23, where a is a constant, the y intercept of C is -12, and (x + 4) is a factor of f(x), find, in simplest form, f(x). (6)
questions.mark_scheme_text: M1: Integrates f'(x) with two correct indices (no requirement for the +c): f(x) = 2x^3 + (1/2)ax^2 - 23x + c. A1: Fully correct integration (may be unsimplified); the +c must be seen (or implied by the -12). B1: Deduces that the constant term ('c') is -12 (from the y-intercept). dM1: Dependent upon having done some integration; sets up a linear equation in a by using f(-4) = 0 (since (x+4) is a factor), e.g. 2(-4)^3 + (1/2)a(-4)^2 - 23(-4) - 12 = 0 (may also be scored via long division, requiring a complete method leading to a remainder in terms of a which is set = 0). dM1: Solves the linear equation in a (dependent upon having attempted integration and used f(-4)=0, or long division/comparing coefficients with (x+4) as a factor). A1cso: f(x) = 2x^3 + 3x^2 - 23x - 12, or equivalent e.g. (x+4)(2x^2-5x-3) or (x+4)(2x+1)(x-3) ('f(x) =' does not need to be seen; ignore any '= 0'). (6 marks)

questions.question_text:
A quantity of ethanol was heated until it reached boiling point. The temperature of the ethanol, θ °C, at time t seconds after heating began, is modelled by the equation θ = A - B e^(-0.07t), where A and B are positive constants. Given that the initial temperature of the ethanol was 18 °C, and after 10 seconds the temperature of the ethanol was 44 °C,
(a) find a complete equation for the model, giving the values of A and B to 3 significant figures. (4)
Ethanol has a boiling point of approximately 78 °C.
(b) Use this information to evaluate the model. (2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Makes the first key step in the solution — substitutes t=0, θ=18 (or t=10, θ=44) into the equation of the model to obtain an equation connecting A and B (note that 18 = A - B e^0 scores M0 unless 18 = A - B is seen or implied later). M1: Substitutes both t=0,θ=18 and t=10,θ=44 to obtain 2 equations connecting A and B, and proceeds to solve them simultaneously to obtain values for both constants. A1: A = awrt 70 or B = awrt 52 (at least one correct). A1: θ = 69.6 - 51.6e^(-0.07t) — must be a fully correct equation as shown (allow recovery if seen in part (b)). (4 marks)
(b) B1ft: Identifies A as the boiling point/maximum temperature in the model (follow through their A), e.g. 'the maximum temperature is 69.6°C according to the model' / 'the model has an upper limit of 69.6°C'. B1ft: Makes a valid conclusion (valid/not valid, good/not good) that refers to the 78 and includes a reference to a significant/large difference, e.g. 'model is not appropriate as 69.6°C is much lower than 78°C' (minimum for both marks). An alternative route, provided their A<78, is: θ=78 => 51.6e^(-0.07t) = 69.6-78 = -8.4, noting the equation cannot be solved, e.g. cannot take the log of a negative number — condone numerical slips. Note B0B1 is not possible. (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
In this question you must show all stages of your working. Solutions relying entirely on calculator technology are not acceptable.
(a) Show that cos 3A ≡ 4 cos^3 A - 3 cos A. (4)
(b) Hence solve, for -90° ≤ x ≤ 180°, the equation 1 - cos 3x = sin^2 x. (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts to use the compound angle formula for cos(2A+A) [or cos(A+2A)]: cos 3A = cos 2A cos A - sin 2A sin A (condone a slip in sign). dM1: Uses correct double angle identities for cos 2A and sin 2A: (2cos^2A - 1)cosA - (2 sinA cosA) sinA (cos2A = 2cos^2A-1 must be used; depends on previous mark). ddM1: Attempts to get all terms in terms of cos A using correct and appropriate identities, e.g. (2cos^2A-1)cosA - 2cosA(1-cos^2A) (replacing sin^2A by 1-cos^2A; depends on both previous marks). A1*: A completely correct and rigorous proof, with correct notation, no mixed variables or missing brackets, leading to 4cos^3A - 3cosA. (4 marks)
(b) M1: Forms an equation just in cos x, using part (a) and the identity sin^2 x = 1 - cos^2 x: cos 2x + 3cos x - 4cos^3 x = 0 (allow one slip in sign or coefficient when copying the result from part (a)). dM1: Dependent on the preceding mark — takes the cubic equation in cos x and makes a valid attempt to solve it (e.g. factorising cos x(4cos^2x - cos x - 3) = 0 => cos x(4cos x + 3)(cos x - 1) = 0), reaching at least one non-zero value for cos x. A1: Two of -90°, 0, 90°, awrt 139°. A1: All four of -90°, 0, 90°, awrt 139°, with no extra solutions offered within the range. (4 marks)

questions.question_text:
Figure 2 shows a sketch of the graph with equation y = 2|x + 4| - 5. The vertex of the graph is at the point P, shown in Figure 2.
(a) Find the coordinates of P. (2)
(b) Solve the equation 3x + 40 = 2|x + 4| - 5. (2)
A line l has equation y = ax, where a is a constant. Given that l intersects y = 2|x + 4| - 5 at least once,
(c) find the range of possible values of a, writing your answer in set notation. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: One correct coordinate — either x = -4 or y = -5 (or (-4, ...) or (..., -5) seen). B1: Deduces that P(-4, -5) (accept written separately e.g. x=-4, y=-5). (2 marks)
(b) M1: Attempts to solve 3x + 40 = -2(x+4) - 5 => x = ... (must reach a value for x; an attempt that is later crossed out can still count). A1: x = -10.6, oe e.g. -53/5 only (if other values are given, e.g. x=-37, they must be rejected or -53/5 clearly chosen as the answer; ignore any attempts to find y). Correct answer with no working scores both marks. (2 marks)
(c) B1: Deduces that a > 2. M1: Attempts to find a value for a using their P(-4,-5): y = ax => -5 = -4a => a = 5/4 (alternatively attempts to solve ax=2(x+4)-5 for the tangency/touching condition). A1: Correct range in acceptable set notation, e.g. {a : a ≤ 1.25} ∪ {a : a > 2}. (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
Figure 3 shows a sketch of the curve with parametric equations x = 6 sin t, y = 5 sin 2t, 0 ≤ t ≤ pi/2. The region R, shown shaded in Figure 3, is bounded by the curve and the x-axis.
(a) (i) Show that the area of R is given by ∫[0 to pi/2] 60 sin t cos^2 t dt. (3)
(ii) Hence show, by algebraic integration, that the area of R is exactly 20. (3)
Figure 4 shows part of the curve used to model the profile of a small dam. Using the model and given that x and y are in metres, the vertical wall of the dam is 4.2 metres high, and there is a horizontal walkway of width MN along the top of the dam,
(b) calculate the width of the walkway. (5)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a)(i) M1: Attempts to multiply y by dx/dt to obtain A sin 2t cos t (may apply sin 2t = 2 sin t cos t here): 5 sin 2t × 6 cos t. dM1: Attempts to use sin 2t = 2 sin t cos t within an integral (may be implied by e.g. ∫A sin 2t × cos t dt = ∫k sin t cos^2 t dt). A1*: Fully correct work leading to the given answer — must include sin 2t = 2 sin t cos t (or e.g. 5 sin 2t = 10 sin t cos t) seen explicitly, and a correct intermediate line that includes an integral sign and the 'dt' (the limits may just 'appear' in the final answer). (3 marks)
(a)(ii) M1: Obtains ∫60 sin t cos^2 t dt = k cos^3 t (may be attempted via a substitution u = cos t to obtain ∫60 sin t cos^2 t dt = k u^3). A1: Correct integration -20 cos^3 t (or equivalent e.g. -20u^3). A1*: Rigorous proof with all aspects correct, including the correct limits and the '0 - (-20)' step, Area = [-20cos^3 t] from 0 to pi/2 = 0 - (-20) = 20. (3 marks)
(b) M1: Uses the given model and attempts to find value(s) of t when sin 2t = 4.2/5, e.g. 2t = sin^(-1)(4.2/5) => t = ... A1: At least one correct value for t, correct to 2dp: t = 0.4986..., 1.072... (or in degrees, 28.57°, 61.42°). dM1: Attempts to find TWO distinct values of x when sin 2t = 4.2/5 (condone poor trig work; allow this mark if 2 values of x are attempted from 2 values of t). A1: Both values of x correct to 2dp: x = 2.869..., 5.269... A1: Width of walkway = 2.40 metres (allow awrt 2.40m, 2.4m — not awrt 2.4m, or awrt 240cm; units required). (5 marks)

questions.question_text:
The function g is defined by g(x) = (3 ln(x) - 7)/(ln(x) - 2), x > 0, x ≠ k, where k is a constant.
(a) Deduce the value of k. (1)
(b) Prove that g'(x) > 0 for all values of x in the domain of g. (3)
(c) Find the range of values of a for which g(a) > 0. (2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: Deduces k = e^2 (or x ≠ e^2; condone k = awrt 7.39). (1 mark)
(b) M1: Attempts to differentiate via the quotient rule, with d/dx(ln x) = 1/x, allowing for g'(x) = [(ln x - 2)×α/x - (3ln x - 7)×β/x] / (ln x - 2)^2, α,β > 0 (a correct rule may be implied by their u, v, u', v' followed by applying (vu'-uv')/v^2; also allow equivalent chain-rule or product-rule approaches, e.g. writing g(x) = 3 - (ln x - 2)^(-1) or g(x) = (3ln x - 7)(ln x - 2)^(-1); condone missing brackets for this mark). A1: Numerator simplifies to 1/x, giving g'(x) = 1/(x(ln x - 2)^2) (allow a correctly expanded denominator; may be established with numerator and denominator found independently). A1cso: States that as x > 0 (or 1/x > 0) AND (ln x - 2) is squared, so g'(x) > 0 for all x in the domain of g. (3 marks)
(c) M1: Attempts to solve either 3 ln a - 7 = 0 or ln a - 2 = 0 (or the corresponding inequality, e.g. 3 ln a - 7 > 0) to reach a value for a (may be given as an inequality, e.g. a > ...). A1: 0 < a < e^2, a > e^(7/3). (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
A circle C with radius r lies only in the 1st quadrant and touches the x-axis and touches the y-axis. The line l has equation 2x + y = 12.
(a) Show that the x coordinates of the points of intersection of l with C satisfy 5x^2 + (2r - 48)x + (r^2 - 24r + 144) = 0. (3)
Given also that l is a tangent to C,
(b) find the two possible values of r, giving your answers as fully simplified surds. (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: Deduces the correct equation of the circle: (x-r)^2 + (y-r)^2 = r^2, or x^2+y^2-2rx-2ry+r^2=0 (since a circle of radius r lying only in the first quadrant and touching both axes has centre (r,r)). M1: Attempts to form an equation with terms of the form x^2, x, r^2, and xr only, using y = 12 - 2x substituted into their circle equation (which must be of an appropriate form, i.e. includes or implies x^2, y^2, r^2). A1*: Uses correct and accurate algebra leading to the given solution 5x^2 + (2r-48)x + (r^2-24r+144) = 0. (3 marks)
(b) M1: Attempts to use b^2 - 4ac ... 0 (where ... is '=' or an inequality) with a=5, b=2r-48, c=r^2-24r+144 (allow minor slips when copying a, b, c provided it does not make the work easier). A1: Correct quadratic equation in r (or inequality), terms collected: r^2 - 18r + 36 = 0, or any multiple of this. dM1: Correct attempt to solve their 3-term quadratic in r (dependent on previous M), e.g. (r-9)^2 - 81 + 36 = 0 => r = ... A1: r = 9 ± 3sqrt(5), careful and accurate work leading to both answers in the required (simplified surd) form. (4 marks)

questions.question_text:
In this question you must show all stages of your working. Solutions relying entirely on calculator technology are not acceptable.
A geometric series has common ratio r and first term a. Given r ≠ 1 and a ≠ 0,
(a) prove that Sn = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r). (4)
Given also that S10 is four times S5,
(b) find the exact value of r. (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: Writes out the sum or lists terms: Sn = a + ar + ar^2 + ... + ar^(n-1) (condone the omission of 'S'; the sum must include the first and last terms and at least two other correct terms and no incorrect terms, e.g. ar^n; may be seen embedded within their working). M1: For the key step of attempting to multiply the first series by r and subtracting: rSn = ar + ar^2 + ar^3 + ... + ar^n => Sn - rSn = ... A1: Sn - rSn = a - ar^n, either way around (condone one side being prematurely factorised, but not both, following correct work). A1*: Depends on all previous marks — proceeds to the given result Sn = a(1-r^n)/(1-r), showing all steps including seeing both sides unfactorised at some point in their working. (4 marks)
(b) M1: For the correct strategy of producing an equation in just r^10 and r^5 (and possibly (1-r)) with the '4' on either side, using the result from part (a), and makes progress to at least cancel through by a: a(1-r^10)/(1-r) = 4 × a(1-r^5)/(1-r). A1: Correct equation with the a and the (1-r) cancelled: 1 - r^10 = 4(1 - r^5) (allow any correct equivalent equation in just r^5 and r^10). dM1: Depends on the first M — solves as far as r^5 = ... by solving a 3-term quadratic in r^5 (e.g. r^10 - 4r^5 + 3 = 0 => (r^5-1)(r^5-3) = 0 => r^5 = ...) by a valid method, or by difference of two squares. A1: r = fifth root of 3 (i.e. r = 3^(1/5)), oe only (the solution r = 1, if found, must be rejected here since r ≠ 1 is given). (4 marks)

questions.question_text: Use algebra to prove that the square of any natural number is either a multiple of 3 or one more than a multiple of 3. (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text: M1: Makes the key step of attempting to write the natural numbers in any 2 of the 3 distinct forms 3k, 3k+1, 3k+2 (or equivalent expressions, e.g. 3k-1, 3k, 3k+1) and attempts to square these expressions. A1 (M1 on EPEN): Successfully shows for 2 cases that the squares are either a multiple of 3 or one more than a multiple of 3, using algebra made explicit, e.g. (3k)^2 = 9k^2 = 3×(3k^2), a multiple of 3; (3k+1)^2 = 9k^2+6k+1 = 3(3k^2+2k)+1, one more than a multiple of 3; (3k+2)^2 = 9k^2+12k+4 = 3(3k^2+4k+1)+1, one more than a multiple of 3 (also allow other rigorous arguments, e.g. '9k^2 is a multiple of 3 and 6k is a multiple of 3 so 9k^2+6k+1 is one more than a multiple of 3'). M1 (A1 on EPEN): Recognises that all natural numbers can be written in one of the 3 distinct forms (or equivalent expressions) and attempts to square in all 3 cases. A1: Successfully shows for all 3 cases that the squares are either a multiple of 3 or one more than a multiple of 3 using algebra, and makes a conclusion (allow tick, QED etc.). (4 marks)
